platforms.title: How Much of the Weight You Lose on Wegovy Is Actually Muscle?
platforms.meta_description: DXA scans from the STEP 1 and SURMOUNT-1 trials measured it. Here is the real fat-to-lean split, and the two habits that protect muscle on a GLP-1.
platforms.body_html:
The scale has moved 12 kilos in the right direction and your clothes finally fit — but your arms look thinner than you wanted, the stairs feel heavier than they did, and you have started wondering whether some of what left was muscle. It is a fair question, and it has a real answer: the body-composition scans built into the semaglutide and tirzepatide trials measured exactly this. The numbers are less alarming than the headlines, and more actionable.

What the DXA Scans Actually Showed

In the STEP 1 trial of semaglutide 2.4 mg, a subgroup of 140 participants had dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) scans at baseline and week 68. Body weight fell 15.0 percent. Within that, total fat mass fell 19.3 percent and total lean body mass fell 9.7 percent, while regional visceral fat dropped 27.4 percent. Because fat fell faster than lean tissue, the proportion of the body that was lean actually rose by 3.0 percentage points. Spain's medicines agency, the AEMPS, reviewed the same substudy in its therapeutic positioning report and concluded the weight loss could be attributed principally to a reduction in adipose tissue.

The tirzepatide picture is similar. In the SURMOUNT-1 body-composition substudy of 160 adults, body weight fell 21.3 percent at week 72, fat mass 33.9 percent and lean mass 10.9 percent. Translated into a ratio, roughly 75 percent of the weight lost was fat and 25 percent was lean mass — and, importantly, that split was the same in the placebo group. Losing some lean tissue is what happens in any substantial weight loss, whether it comes from a drug, a diet, or surgery.

Two caveats are worth holding onto. First, "lean mass" on a DXA scan is not the same thing as muscle: it includes body water, organs and connective tissue, and some of the early drop is fluid rather than contractile tissue. Second, these were exploratory analyses in small subgroups, not the trials' primary endpoints. They tell you the direction of travel, not a precise personal forecast.

Why the Body Reaches for Muscle at All

Semaglutide acts on GLP-1 receptors in the hypothalamus and brainstem; tirzepatide adds GIP receptor activity. Both dial down appetite and slow gastric emptying, so intake falls sharply and often without the person noticing how sharply. When energy intake drops well below what the body is spending, protein from skeletal muscle becomes one of the fuels it draws on. Sweden's Livsmedelsverket puts the mechanism plainly in its guidance on protein: if the body does not get enough energy, protein is used as an energy source instead of as building material.

This is why the licensed indication itself is not "take the injection." Both the FDA-approved labels for Wegovy and Zepbound and the EU labels describe these medicines as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. The diet and the training are not a bonus tacked onto the prescription; they are the conditions under which the drug was studied and approved.

Skip the Muscle-Loss Panic — Here Is What Actually Protects Lean Mass

Two levers do most of the work, and neither of them is a supplement.

  • Protein, spread across the day. The US Recommended Dietary Allowance is 0.8 g per kilogram of body weight per day, which is a floor for a weight-stable adult, not a target for someone in a steep deficit. Systematic reviews of energy-restricted diets consistently find that intakes in the region of 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg per day preserve lean mass better than 0.8 g/kg, and obesity-medicine practice guidance uses that range. When appetite is suppressed, the practical move is to build each smaller meal around the protein — eggs, fish, poultry, dairy, tofu, beans — rather than filling the plate with bread, rice or pasta and hoping protein arrives later.
  • Resistance training, at least twice a week. The US Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans call for muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week, in addition to aerobic activity. Loading a muscle is the signal that tells the body to keep it. Without that signal, tissue that is not being used is the first thing an energy-short body is willing to give up. Bodyweight squats, push-ups and resistance bands count; a gym membership is not the requirement.

One thing you will see quoted online is worth handling carefully: a 2025 case series reported three patients on semaglutide or tirzepatide who trained 3 to 5 days a week and ate high protein, with lean soft tissue changes of −6.9, +2.5 and +5.8 percent. Three people is a case series, not evidence that most trainers gain muscle — and one of the three still lost lean tissue. The direction is encouraging; the numbers are not a promise.

The Part Most People Underestimate: Stopping

The STEP 1 extension, published by Wilding and colleagues in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism in 2022, followed 327 participants for a year after treatment ended. Mean weight loss at week 68 had been 17.3 percent. By week 120, participants had regained 11.6 percentage points — about two-thirds of what they had lost — leaving a net 5.6 percent below baseline, with most cardiometabolic improvements drifting back toward starting values. Nearly half, 48.2 percent, were still at least 5 percent down.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis in The BMJ, led by researchers at Oxford's Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, pooled 37 studies covering more than 9,000 adults who came off weight-management medication. Regain averaged 0.4 kg per month overall and around 0.8 kg per month for semaglutide and tirzepatide, a trajectory that returns most people to their starting weight in roughly a year and a half.

None of that is a reason to stop or change a dose on your own. Whether, when and how to come off one of these medicines — including whether the dose is stepped down — is a clinical decision for the prescriber, and the sensible time to ask about the plan is at the start of treatment rather than the week you decide you are done. What you control in the meantime is the part that carries over: if the protein habit and the twice-weekly lifting are already established before the last injection, they are still there afterwards.

If you take one thing from all of this, make it the training. Protein without a loading stimulus is just calories; two short strength sessions a week are what turn the food you eat into muscle you keep.

This article is general health information and not medical advice. Decisions about prescription medicines, including starting, adjusting or stopping them, belong with your doctor or pharmacist.
